subject: Histology
concept: Platelets (thrombocytes) are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments released from mature megakaryocytes in bone marrow and are central to primary hemostasis.

content.definition: Platelets are small, anucleate cytoplasmic fragments derived from mature megakaryocytes. They circulate in blood and rapidly respond to vascular injury.
content.explanation: In resting blood, platelets are discoid. After vascular injury they adhere to exposed subendothelial structures, become activated, release granule contents, change shape and aggregate to form the primary hemostatic plug.
content.mechanism: Thrombopoiesis occurs mainly in bone marrow. Hematopoietic stem cells generate megakaryocytic progenitors, which mature into megakaryocytes. Thrombopoietin is the major regulator of megakaryocyte and platelet production. Megakaryocytes undergo endomitosis and become highly polyploid, extend proplatelet processes toward marrow sinusoids, and release platelets.
content.structure: Resting platelets are discoid and approximately 2–4 micrometers in diameter. They lack a nucleus but contain mitochondria, glycogen, a marginal microtubule band, a dense tubular system, an open canalicular system, and secretory granules. Alpha granules contain proteins involved in hemostasis, adhesion, inflammation and repair; dense granules contain mediators including ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin.
content.function: Platelets mediate primary hemostasis through adhesion, activation, secretion and aggregation. Activated platelets also provide a procoagulant phospholipid surface that supports coagulation reactions and contributes to fibrin formation and stabilization.
content.clinical_relevance: Reduced platelet number causes thrombocytopenia and may impair primary hemostasis. Increased platelet number is thrombocytosis. Platelet function disorders can cause bleeding despite a normal platelet count.
content.diagnosis: Evaluation commonly begins with a complete blood count and peripheral blood smear. Depending on the clinical context, platelet function studies and coagulation testing may be added.
content.treatment: Management of platelet disorders is cause-directed and depends on whether the problem is reduced platelet production, increased destruction or consumption, increased platelet number, or abnormal platelet function.
high_yield: Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments, not complete nucleated cells.
They are released from mature megakaryocytes, primarily in bone marrow.
Thrombopoietin is the major regulator of thrombopoiesis.
Megakaryocytes undergo endomitosis and polyploidization before platelet release.
Platelets form a primary hemostatic plug through adhesion, activation, secretion and aggregation.
Alpha granules contain proteins involved in hemostasis, adhesion, inflammation and tissue repair.
Dense granules contain ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin.
Typical platelet lifespan is about 7–10 days.

terminology.etymology: From platelet, a small plate-like cell fragment.
terminology.notes: Anucleate blood element involved in primary hemostasis.
